extracted.intended_audience: Voters and the general public of New York (readers of the Federalist Papers); citizens deliberating adoption of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_short: arguing for a stronger national constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of late-18th-century political essays (Federalist Papers Nos. 15–18) arguing that the Articles of Confederation are insufficient and that a national Constitution must give the Union direct, enforceable powers over individuals rather than only over states. The pieces explain structural defects of confederacies and prescribe characteristics a viable national government must possess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation_should_apply_to_individuals_not_only_states
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is in the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, and as contradistinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functioning national government must be able to make laws that operate directly upon citizens rather than only issuing requisitions or recommendations to state governments. When laws are framed only for states as corporate bodies, they become optional in practice and lack effective enforcement; this principle is identified as the root cause of weakness in the Confederation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority_to_raise_men_and_money_directly_from_citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: “Except as to the rule of appointment, the United States has an indefinite discretion to make requisitions for men and money; but they have no authority to raise either, by regulations extending to the individual citizens of America.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national government must possess explicit power to levy resources (troops, funds) by regulations aimed at individuals; reliance on state compliance via requisitions produces inconsistent and insufficient contributions and cripples national action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws_must_be_attended_with_sanctions_enforceable_by_courts_not_depend_on_military_coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Government implies the power of making laws. It is essential to the idea of a law, that it be attended with a sanction; or, in other words, a penalty or punishment for disobedience... This penalty... can only be inflicted in two ways: by the agency of the courts and ministers of justice, or by military force; by the COERCION of the magistracy, or by the COERCION of arms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer civil/magisterial enforcement (courts, ordinary magistracy) so laws bind individuals. Designs that leave enforcement to military force (against states as collective bodies) risk civil war, tyranny, impracticability, or dependence on a standing army and are therefore unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: National_government_must_possess_energy_and_adequate_powers
rubrics_metrics.description: “They admit that the government of the United States is destitute of energy, they contend against conferring upon it those powers which are requisite to supply that energy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A viable constitution must give the Union sufficient powers (commerce, finance, negotiation, war, etc.) to act effectively. Sparing the national government necessary powers to preserve public order and effect policy leaves the Union impotent and unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_dependence_on_state_intervention_for_execution_of_national_laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “It must stand in need of no intermediate legislations; but must itself be empowered to employ the arm of the ordinary magistrate to execute its own resolutions... If the execution of the laws of the national government should not require the intervention of the State legislatures, the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exertion of an unconstitutional power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design national measures to operate immediately on citizens so state legislatures cannot defeat them by omission, evasion, or procedural delay. Reliance on state intermediaries allows subtle non-compliance and undermines uniform national policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do_not_require_concurrence_of_many_distinct_sovereign_wills
rubrics_metrics.description: “In our case, the concurrence of thirteen distinct sovereign wills is requisite, under the Confederation, to the complete execution of every important measure that proceeds from the Union.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A system that effectively permits many separate sovereign entities to veto or block national measures will stall government; constitutional design must reduce the number or effect of separate sovereign vetoes so the Union can act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account_for_human_nature_faction_and_local_self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “Why has government been instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not conform to the dictates of reason and justice, without constraint... A spirit of faction... will often hurry the persons of whom they are composed into improprieties and excesses... Power controlled or abridged is almost always the rival and enemy of that power by which it is controlled or abridged.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional structure must be realistic about human motives: do not presume that state leaders or assemblies will subordinate narrow local interests to national good. Design must include institutional checks and modes of direct national operation to counteract faction and the love of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties_and_leagues_without_effective_sanctions_are_unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing absurd or impracticable in the idea of a league or alliance... leaving nothing to future discretion; and depending for its execution on the good faith of the parties... they were scarcely formed before they were broken... how little dependence is to be placed on treaties which have no other sanction than the obligations of good faith.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangements that depend solely on mutual good faith and lack enforceable sanctions tend to fail; a national government must have institutional mechanisms (not merely treaty obligations) to secure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize_state_advantage_through_local_administration_of_justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is one transcendant advantage belonging to the province of the State governments... I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. This, of all others, is the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because states gain strong civic attachment through local justice administration and familiar governance, a national constitution must acknowledge this source of state influence and structure national powers so as to balance, not futilely attempt to wholly supplant, local legitimacy.
